newsitem.title: UK: Inverurie shows all to play for at UK election.
newsitem.headline: Inverurie shows all to play for at UK election.

text.p: With a week to go to Britain's general election, voters in this small town in northern Scotland are proof positive that Prime Minister John Major is down but not yet out.

Although some traditional supporters of Major's ruling Conservative party are disgruntled, especially over health and education, they are wary of throwing in their lot with opposition Labour leader Tony Blair.
And a striking number of voters say they are still undecided whether to return the Conservatives on May 1 for an unprecedented fifth consecutive term of office.

"I don't trust any of them. I don't like the way any of the parties come across," said Wendy Gard, a young mother watching Major press the flesh during a campaign stop on Wednesday in Inverurie, not far from the oil and fishing city of Aberdeen.

Gard, holding a red-cheeked baby in her arms, is worried that her eldest son's education is suffering because he is in a class of 33. But, as someone who has never known a Labour government, she frets that opposition leader Tony Blair is an unknown quantity.
"What will Labour do? Will they be any different? I'll probably stick with the Conservatives -- better the devil you know than the devil you don't know," she said.

Her friend, Caroline Taylor, says she too will probably stick with the Conservatives, largely because of fears that Labour's left-wing trade union backers will try to push Blair around if he is elected.
"If they're keeping quiet now, waiting for the election, what are they going to do after the election? Why are they keeping quiet now? That's what concerns me," she said.
A middle-aged woman, who like quite a few former Conservative voters declined to give her name, said she was simply annoyed by many of the ruling party's policies.
"There's just a lot of things I don't agree with. The health service is just in a total mess. I haven't decided who I'm going to vote for, you ken (know). I'm just thinking about it," she said.

A man who voted Conservative in 1992 and was also undecided said he was worried, despite Major's increasingly "Euro-sceptic" stance, that the Conservatives were prepared to surrender too much sovereignty to the European Union.

Such views were reflected in an opinion poll released late on Wednesday which showed that while Labour had a 19 point lead over the Conservatives, half of the electorate had not finally made up their mind.
Two other polls showed Labour leads of 20 and 21 points -- much bigger than the five percent margin in a survey for The Guardian newspaper 24 hours earlier.
Inverurie is in the constituency of Gordon, which was won by Britain's third party, the Liberal Democrats, in 1992.

Despite boundary changes that now make it on paper a comfortable Conservative seat, Lib Dem activists said farmers' fury over the government's handling of last year's health scare over beef made them confident they could hang on.
One vote up for grabs is that of Ian Harper, 65, who is leaning towards the pro-independence Scottish Nationalist Party because he is angry with Major for slapping tax on home heating bills.
He also wants to know what the government has done with the tens of billions of pounds raised from privatising vast swathes of the British economy.
"This country, in my opinion, should be really rich. When you think of all the nationalised businesses that have been sold, all the oil... where has the money gone?" Harper asked.
"I've always voted Tory all my life, but I'm going to think about it this time," he added.
